topics.title: Revision of First Term Work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to recall the components of a solar photovoltaic system.
The students should be able to explain the process of system design and sizing.
The students should be able to identify common issues in solar installations.

Introduction:
Last term, we learned about the basic components and installation of solar photovoltaic systems. Today, we will revise those important concepts to ensure everyone has a strong foundation before we move to new topics.

Content:
We will review the main components of a solar PV system: solar panels, charge controllers, batteries, inverters, and mounting structures. Remember, solar panels convert sunlight into direct current (DC) electricity. In our Nigerian context, panels are often installed on rooftops or in open fields where they can receive maximum sunlight, especially during the dry season when we have more sunshine.

System design and sizing involves calculating the energy needs of a household or business and determining how many panels and batteries are required. For example, a typical Nigerian home might need a system that can power lights, fans, and a television. We consider factors like daily sunlight hours and energy consumption patterns.

Common issues include shading problems, loose connections, and battery maintenance. In Nigeria, heavy rain during the wet season can cause water damage if installations are not properly protected.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to design a basic solar system for a small shop in the market. They must calculate the required panels and batteries based on typical shop appliances.

Evaluation questions:
1. Name three main components of a solar PV system.
2. Why is proper system sizing important in solar installation?
3. How does the rainy season affect solar installations in Nigeria?
4. What happens when solar panels are shaded by trees?

Summary:
Today's revision has reinforced our understanding of solar PV system components and design principles, which are essential for proper installation and maintenance.

topics.title: Electrical Wiring for Solar S
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to differentiate between AC and DC cables used in solar systems.
The students should be able to explain the importance of colour coding in electrical wiring.
The students should be able to calculate appropriate cable sizes for different solar components.

Introduction:
After revising the basic components, we now focus on how these components are connected through proper electrical wiring. Just like the nerves in our body carry messages, electrical wiring carries energy in a solar system.

Content:
In solar systems, we use two main types of cables: DC (direct current) cables for connecting solar panels to charge controllers and batteries, and AC (alternating current) cables for connecting inverters to household appliances. In Nigeria, we often use DC cables for the outdoor parts of the system where they are exposed to our harsh weather conditions.

Colour coding is crucial for safety and proper installation. Red or black cables typically carry positive current, while blue or black cables carry negative current. This helps prevent reverse polarity, which can damage equipment. In our practical sessions, we practice connecting these cables properly, just like connecting the positive and negative terminals of a torch battery.

Cable sizing depends on the current flow and distance. Thicker cables are needed for longer distances to minimize voltage drop. For example, connecting solar panels on a rooftop to batteries in the basement requires thicker cables than a short connection. We use formulas to calculate the appropriate cable size based on current and distance.

In Nigerian installations, we must consider our high temperatures which affect cable performance. We also need to protect cables from damage by animals or accidental cutting during construction.

Class activity:
Students will practice connecting solar panels, charge controllers, and batteries using proper colour coding and cable sizing. They will measure voltage drop across different cable lengths.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the difference between AC and DC cables in solar systems?
2. Why is colour coding important in electrical wiring?
3. How do you determine the appropriate cable size for a solar installation?
4. What special considerations should be made for cable installation in Nigeria's climate?

Summary:
Proper electrical wiring is essential for safe and efficient solar system operation, and understanding cable types, colour coding, and sizing ensures reliable performance.

topics.title: Battery Bank Configuration
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate series and parallel connections of batteries.
The students should be able to calculate battery capacity and voltage for different configurations.
The students should be able to explain factors that affect battery performance and lifespan.

Introduction:
Batteries are like the savings account of a solar system, storing energy for use when the sun isn't shining. Today, we learn how to properly configure these batteries to meet different energy needs.

Content:
Batteries in solar systems can be connected in series, parallel, or a combination of both. In series connection, positive terminal of one battery connects to negative terminal of the next, increasing voltage while keeping capacity the same. For example, connecting two 12V batteries in series gives 24V with the same amp-hour rating.

In parallel connection, positive terminals connect together and negative terminals connect together, increasing capacity while keeping voltage the same. Two 12V 100Ah batteries in parallel still give 12V but with 200Ah capacity. In Nigerian homes, we often use 24V systems for better efficiency with larger loads.

Battery capacity is measured in amp-hours (Ah), representing how much current a battery can deliver over time. Voltage determines the electrical pressure. To calculate total capacity, multiply amp-hours by number of batteries in parallel. For voltage, multiply battery voltage by number in series.

Several factors affect battery performance in our Nigerian climate: high temperatures can reduce lifespan, while deep discharges regularly can damage batteries. Proper maintenance includes checking electrolyte levels (for lead-acid batteries), keeping terminals clean, and storing in cool, ventilated areas away from direct sunlight.

Class activity:
Students will build a 24V battery bank using 12V batteries, demonstrating both series and parallel connections while measuring voltage and capacity at each stage.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the difference between series and parallel battery connections?
2. How do you calculate the total voltage of four 12V batteries connected in series?
3. Why is battery maintenance important in Nigeria's climate?
4. What capacity would you get from connecting three 12V 100Ah batteries in parallel?

Summary:
Proper battery bank configuration ensures efficient energy storage and extends battery life, which is crucial for reliable solar power systems.

topics.title: Inverter Operation and Connec
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the functions of an inverter in a solar system.
The students should be able to differentiate between pure sine wave and modified sine wave inverters.
The students should be able to demonstrate proper inverter wiring connections.

Introduction:
While batteries store energy, inverters transform that stored energy into a form our appliances can use. Just as a transformer changes voltage, an inverter changes current type from DC to AC.

Content:
An inverter converts the DC electricity from batteries into AC electricity that powers household appliances. In Nigeria, most of our appliances like refrigerators, fans, and televisions run on AC power, making inverters essential components of solar systems.

There are two main types of inverters: pure sine wave and modified sine wave. Pure sine wave inverters produce smooth, clean electricity identical to what comes from the grid, making them suitable for all appliances including sensitive electronics. Modified sine wave inverters are less expensive but may not work properly with some devices like certain motors or medical equipment. In Nigerian homes, pure sine wave inverters are preferred for their compatibility with all our appliances.

Proper inverter wiring involves connecting DC input from the battery bank with correct polarity and connecting AC output to the distribution board or appliances. Safety precautions include ensuring all power is off during installation, using appropriately sized cables, and providing adequate ventilation as inverters generate heat during operation.

Testing involves checking voltage outputs, load capacity, and automatic transfer functions if the inverter has grid-tie capability. In our Nigerian context, we must also test performance during our frequent power outages to ensure reliable backup power.

Class activity:
Students will connect an inverter to a battery bank and then to various loads, measuring voltage and current at different points to understand power conversion.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the primary function of an inverter in a solar system?
2. What is the difference between pure sine wave and modified sine wave inverters?
3. Why is proper polarity important when connecting an inverter to batteries?
4. What special considerations are needed for inverter installation in Nigeria's climate?

Summary:
Inverters play a crucial role in solar systems by converting stored DC power to usable AC electricity, and proper installation ensures reliable operation of all household appliances.

topics.title: MID-TERM EXAMINATION
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate knowledge of solar photovoltaic system components.
The students should be able to apply concepts of electrical wiring and battery configuration.
The students should be able to solve practical problems related to solar installation.

Introduction:
Today's examination will test your understanding of the topics we've covered so far this term, including system components, electrical wiring, battery configuration, and inverter operation.

Content:
The examination will consist of multiple choice questions, short answer questions, and practical problem-solving exercises. You will need to recall information about solar panel types, cable sizing, battery connections, and inverter specifications.

For the practical section, you will be given scenarios typical of Nigerian solar installations and asked to propose solutions. For example, you might need to design a small system for a rural clinic or troubleshoot a malfunctioning installation.

Remember to apply the safety principles we've discussed throughout the term. Proper installation techniques and safety precautions are as important as technical knowledge in solar photovoltaic work.

Class activity:
Students will complete the examination individually, demonstrating their understanding of solar photovoltaic systems through written responses and problem-solving.

Evaluation questions:
The examination will contain questions covering all topics from weeks 1-4, including:
1. Identification of solar system components
2. Calculation of cable sizes for different loads
3. Battery configuration for specific voltage requirements
4. Inverter selection and connection procedures
5. Troubleshooting common solar system issues

Summary:
This midterm examination assesses your comprehension and application of solar photovoltaic installation concepts covered in the first half of this term.

topics.title: Solar Load Management
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify different types of electrical loads in a solar system.
The students should be able to prioritize loads based on energy availability and importance.
The students should be able to calculate total load consumption for a solar installation.

Introduction:
Even the best solar system is useless if we don't manage how we use the energy it produces. Today, we learn how to make the most of our solar power by understanding and managing our electrical loads.

Content:
Electrical loads are all the devices and appliances that consume power in a solar system. In Nigerian homes, common loads include lighting (LED bulbs, tube lights), entertainment systems (TV, radio), cooling appliances (fans, air conditioners), and kitchen appliances (refrigerators, electric cookers).

Load prioritization is essential because solar systems have limited energy storage. We must decide which loads are most important during periods of low energy production. For example, during our long Harmattan season when sunlight is reduced, we might prioritize lighting and phone charging over entertainment systems.

Estimating total load consumption involves calculating the power rating (watts) of each appliance and multiplying by daily usage hours. For example, a 60W LED bulb used for 5 hours daily consumes 300 watt-hours (0.3 kWh). We add up all these values to determine our total daily energy requirement.

Power rating and efficiency management helps us reduce energy waste. Using energy-efficient appliances like LED instead of incandescent bulbs can significantly reduce our energy needs. In Nigerian markets, we now find many energy-efficient appliances that work well with solar systems.

Class activity:
Students will create a load management plan for a typical Nigerian home, calculating daily energy consumption and prioritizing loads based on importance and energy availability.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is meant by electrical load in a solar system?
2. How do you calculate the daily energy consumption of a 100W television used for 4 hours daily?
3. Why is load prioritization important in solar systems?
4. Name three energy-efficient appliances suitable for Nigerian solar installations.

Summary:
Effective load management maximizes the efficiency and reliability of solar power systems by ensuring energy is used wisely and prioritized according to importance.

topics.title: MID-TERM BREAK
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to rest and prepare for the second half of the term.

Introduction:
After several weeks of intensive learning about solar photovoltaic systems, it's time for a well-deserved break to rest and recharge.

Content:
This mid-term break provides an opportunity for students to relax and reflect on what they've learned so far. It's also a good time to observe solar installations in your communities and notice how they're designed and maintained.

During the break, students might want to review their notes and prepare any questions they have about the topics covered. When we return, we'll continue with more advanced solar installation and maintenance techniques.

Class activity:
Students will enjoy their break with family and friends, returning refreshed and ready to continue their solar photovoltaic studies.

Evaluation questions:
No formal evaluation during the break period.

Summary:
Enjoy your mid-term break and return prepared to continue your solar photovoltaic installation and maintenance studies.
